title: Dogen's Genjokoan, part one
hookLine: read the opening: when all things are Buddha-dharma
tomorrow: how can a whole moon fit inside one drop of water?

cards: Petals drop off the grocery-store flowers on the table, a few more each morning, no matter how much someone loves them. Out back, the weeds come up thick, no matter how much someone hates them.

In Japan, the teacher Dogen wrote an essay called Genjokoan, and its opening section ends on exactly that. In paraphrase: and yet, flowers fall amid our longing, and weeds spread amid our dislike. So then what?
The essay's answer is under your feet.

teach.b: Dogen's opening moves in three steps, and they're worth reading slowly. First: when all things are Buddha-dharma, there is delusion and awakening, practice, birth and death, buddhas and beings. Everything is in play.

teach.h: NO FIXED SELF: NONE OF IT.
teach.b: Second: when all things are without a fixed self, there's no delusion, no awakening, no buddhas, no beings. All of it drops away.

teach.h: LEAPING CLEAR: ALL OF IT AGAIN.
teach.b: Third: the Buddha way leaps clear of both too much and too little, so there is birth and death, delusion and awakening, beings and buddhas after all.
Then the turn: and yet, flowers fall while we long for them, and weeds spread while we dislike them. After all that philosophy, the essay lands in a garden. Dogen doesn't say stop loving flowers.
He doesn't say make peace with weeds and feel nothing.
He says this is what's happening, right here, and practice happens right here too. Then a line that turns the usual direction around.

In paraphrase: carrying the self forward to confirm all things is delusion; all things coming forward and confirming the self is awakening. Not me going out to get the moment. The moment arriving and finding me.
The title holds the idea. Genjo can be read as what's appearing now; koan as a case to be worked through. The case isn't somewhere else.
It's the falling petal. The way is here.

how: The Genjokoan is the opening chapter of many editions of Dogen's Shobogenzo; Soto Zen students study it with teachers, and some read it aloud in retreats.

o: an essay by Dogen on the way as what's appearing now
a riddle Zen students must solve before being ordained
a list of temple rules written by a Japanese abbot

games.q: the opening's steps — tap the pairs.
p: delusion and awakening, all in play

s: Dogen says to stop loving flowers so their falling won't hurt
he just says flowers fall amid our longing and weeds spread amid our dislike. practice happens right there.
in the Genjokoan, carrying the self forward to confirm things is called delusion
awakening is all things coming forward and confirming the self.
the Genjokoan is a Chinese poem
it's an essay by the Japanese Zen teacher Dogen.

games.q: your mom keeps saying she'll start her art class 'once life calms down.' what would Dogen's opening say?
o: the way is here: practice happens in the busy life, not after it.
she's right; real practice needs a calm, quiet time to begin.
she should drop the class; wanting it is just more longing.
games.why: flowers fall and weeds spread anyway. the opening sets practice right in that garden, not in a calmer one later.

practice: Stand up if you can, or sit tall, and feel your feet on the floor. Let the floor come up to meet you: its hardness, its coolness, the small shifts of weight.
Don't go looking for anything special; let what's here arrive, petal and weed alike, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Dogen's Genjokoan: an essay by the Japanese Zen teacher Dogen, read as the case of what is appearing right now. Today, its opening.

orig.note: Japanese: genjō, what is appearing now; kōan, a case to be worked through; the essay's title.

carryVoice: One line for today: the way is here, falling petals and all. Part one, read slowly.

sources.ref: Dogen, Shobogenzo, Genjokoan (opening section: three sentences and 'flowers fall amid our longing, weeds spread amid our dislike'; carrying the self forward vs. all things coming forward)
